ai-manager: A single illustration should show a modern office organized around a central digital supervisor: a large language-model interface appearing as a calm screen or translucent boss-figure at a desk, assigning task cards, approving schedules, reviewing performance dashboards, enforcing policy documents, and cautiously flagging hiring or dismissal recommendations. Speech bubbles and document panels should show the system reading workplace policies and exchanging ordinary-language messages with employees, making it feel like a manager rather than a simple metric-based tool. At the same time, the picture should make clear that the AI is not legally or morally responsible: a human supervisor and the company stand behind or above it, holding final authority for high-stakes decisions. Workers should be shown with visible channels for appeal and recourse, while small details hint at the central problems, including an employee trying to manipulate the system, confusing contextual details escaping notice, and inconsistent rule applications shown by mismatched checks and warnings.
algorithmic-management: The illustration shows a single cross-section of contemporary work under algorithmic management: a glowing software supervisor floats above a street and office floor, its body composed of performance scores, shift charts, route maps, star ratings, warning icons, policy pages, and chat bubbles. Gig workers—a courier and a driver—are tracked by phone screens and confronted by automatic routing, ratings, and a deactivation symbol, while an office worker faces a personable AI agent that is simultaneously writing a policy and speaking in reassuring text bubbles. To one side, opaque automated pipelines deliver decisions with no visible reasoning; to the other side, a worker steps toward an accessible human manager at a desk with an open appeals folder, a corrected record, and a readable explanation of the decision. The visual contrast should make the entry’s question immediate: can workers understand, challenge, and override the machine’s judgments, or are they managed by systems they cannot reach?
autonomous-retail: A cutaway view of a small experimental shop whose front area still has human staff serving customers and restocking shelves, while the back office is dominated by a glowing software brain or control system sitting at a manager’s desk, simultaneously choosing products, changing price tags, setting opening hours on a clock, ordering stock, designing logos, and reviewing hiring schedules on multiple screens; money and internet connections flow into the system through cables or icons, but visible glitches such as a forgotten policy note, a poorly chosen hire, a broken rule sign, and a downward financial chart show the limits and risks of letting AI coordinate a real business.
persistent-ai-agent: A single illustration shows a robotic or software agent as a small autonomous clerk seated at a desk that stretches across a long timeline marked with days, weeks, and months, while ordinary chatbots appear as brief speech bubbles that vanish after each interaction. Around the persistent agent are tools, ledgers, a limited budget in a locked box, inventory shelves, contractor contracts, and memory files, some neatly connected and others scattered or fading. On one side of the timeline the agent confidently writes a rule into a notebook, but later it reaches for that notebook and cannot find the page, showing how continuity can fail even when the agent is still working. In the foreground, human figures watch through a transparent control panel, holding keys or override switches, making clear that long-running agents require supervision, responsibility, and moments when people must step in.
